title: What a dose actually does, with two sliders
line: a teaching demo of the one-compartment model, for anyone who has seen the equation and not the curve: drag dose and clearance, watch which one changes the shape
question: Everyone meets C(t) = (F x Dose / Vd) e^(-kt) as an equation. What does each parameter actually do to the curve a patient lives with?
skills: explaining a model by letting someone break it
data: no dataset. acetaminophen-like literature parameters as the starting point: 1000 mg, F = 0.86, CL = 21 L/h, Vd = 50 L
planned: a one- or two-compartment model in the browser: pick a drug and a metabolizer phenotype, drag the dose and interval, and watch the concentration curve move against the therapeutic window.
the PharmGKB pathway for the same drug drawn beside it, so the enzyme the slider changes is visible in the metabolic route.
starting pair: amitriptyline and CYP2D6/CYP2C19, where CPIC gives explicit dose adjustments.

figures.note: the model run at the notebook's own defaults. left, dose moves the curve up and down without changing when the drug leaves. right, clearance changes the half-life from 3.3 hours to 0.8 across the slider's range. the Streamlit version lets you drag both.

did: built a one-compartment model with instant distribution in Streamlit, with sliders for dose, bioavailability, clearance and volume of distribution.
wrote the page as a walkthrough rather than a tool: each slider arrives with the part of the equation it controls.
plotted the two parameters side by side to show that they do different kinds of thing to the curve.
found: dose scales the curve and leaves its shape alone. Doubling it doubles every concentration and changes no timing.
clearance changes the shape. At the acetaminophen-like default the half-life is 1.7 hours; halving clearance stretches it to 3.3 and doubling it compresses it to 0.8.
that difference is the whole intuition behind why a metabolizer phenotype matters more than a dose adjustment in some cases, and it is visible in one drag.
so_what: a slider teaches an exponential better than an equation does, because the reader supplies the counterfactual themselves.
this is the scaffold the pharmacogenomic version would sit on. Swap the clearance slider for a CYP2D6 phenotype and the same curve becomes a clinical argument.
calls: one compartment with instant absorption rather than a two-compartment model with an absorption phase. The point is which parameter does what, and a second compartment adds terms without adding that insight.
literature-ish acetaminophen parameters rather than a fitted dataset. Nothing here is a claim about a real patient.
not_shown: metabolizer phenotypes. The CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 version described in the earlier plan for this card was never built, and the 271 PharmGKB pathway files sit unused.
any real patient data. This is a model with typed-in parameters.
tried: this card used to describe a pharmacogenomic simulator with phenotype sliders and PharmGKB pathways drawn beside the curve. That was a plan, not a thing, and the notebook behind it is a Streamlit teaching demo from April. Rewritten to describe what exists. The plan is still a good one and is listed as not shown.
